title: Monetary Policy Report—October 2025
summary: The Bank of Canada's October 2025 Monetary Policy Report assesses the Canadian economy as adjusting to steep US tariffs, which have reduced demand for Canadian goods and slowed growth, while underlying inflation remains at approximately 2.5% against a 2% total inflation target. The Bank projects Canadian economic growth strengthening from approximately 0.75% in H2 2025 to annual averages of 1.4% over 2026 and 2027, with total inflation expected to remain near the 2% target over the projection horizon. The report accompanies the Bank's decision to lower the overnight policy rate by 25 basis points to 2.25%.
key_points: US tariffs have led to a fall in demand for Canadian goods, with exports and business investment slumping
CPI inflation was 2.4% in September 2025, up from near 2% for several months, with underlying inflation at approximately 2.5%
Bank of Canada reduced its overnight policy rate by 25 basis points to 2.25% (Bank Rate at 2.5%, deposit rate at 2.20%)
Canadian economic growth projected to strengthen from ~0.75% in H2 2025, averaging 1.4% annually over 2026-2027
Total inflation expected to remain around 2% over the projection horizon despite upward cost pressures from tariffs and trade reconfiguration
Trade-related risks remain elevated, with the ongoing trade conflict expected to have a lasting negative impact on economic activity
why_it_matters: This quarterly monetary policy report from the Bank of Canada provides the official assessment of economic conditions and the policy outlook for Canada's central bank. For traders and analysts, the report signals how the Bank of Canada is navigating the tension between growth headwinds from US tariffs and inflation remaining near target. The rate cut decision signals a dovish tilt in policy as the economy copes with trade disruptions. The forward projections on growth and inflation inform expectations for future policy rate decisions.
macro_context: The report situates Canada's economy within the broader context of US tariff disruptions reshaping global trade flows. While global growth has been resilient, the historic rise in US tariffs is weighing on global growth prospects and pushing up US inflation. Canada's outlook is shaped by two competing forces: tariff-induced weakness in demand versus cost-push pressures from supply chain reconfigurations. The Bank appears to be prioritizing growth support over near-term inflation risks, as evidenced by the rate cut.

issues_found: Minor semantic issue: Summary states 'underlying inflation remains near the 2.5% target' — source indicates total inflation target is 2%, with underlying inflation running at about 2½% (not a separate target)
